and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Twenty Fourth Report of the Committee. This
Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2012-2013) of the Ministry of Environment and
Forests (Demand No. 30).
2. In its meeting of the Committee held on the 11

Officers of the Ministry of Environment and Forests gave an overview of the various activities of
the Ministry and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the
Ministry to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Ministry for replying to the
clarifications sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and Forests.

INTRODUCTORY
Environment in ancient India was not an entity isolated, apart and independent from
mankind. It is rather a modern day phenomenon arising out of crass commercialization, careless
technology, unplanned urbanisation, unbridled human greed, phenomenonal population growth, etc.
Relationship between people and the environment/ecosystem in ancient India had been one of
harmony, coexistence, mutual care and concern – the two supporting and complementing each
other in their own way. This was the reason why respect and care for environment was
intrinsically and inveterately imbedded and imbibed in our way of life and not as a separate activity
or added effort. Worship and reverence to various elements of environment – the earth, air, water
river, tree, forests, mountains, etc. by personifying them not only signify how crucial and vital
these were considered for our existence by our forefathers but also guide us how best to preserve
and protect our environment even in the absence of regulatory regime/environmental governance.
2. Ruefully reverting back to that ideal old age is what now can only be imagined not realized
or redeemed. But, at the same time, environment continues to be as relevant and as important if
not more, in our life as it was in the past and its importance cannot be undermined. The delicate
balance and harmony between economic, social and environmental needs, need to be maintained in
right earnest as the fallout of our casual and callous approach to and utter neglect of environmental
concerns has started manifesting in the form of climate change which may lead to disruptions of
livelihoods, economic activity, living conditions and human health. The above objective can no more
be achieved only through voluntary efforts but a mix of environmental regulations, governance and
management strategies is needed to achieve it.
Mandate and Organizational Structure of the Ministry
3. The Ministry of Environment and Forests is the nodal agency of the Central Government
for planning, promotion, formulation and implementation of environment and forests policies and
programmes with a view to protection of environment, abatement of pollution and conservation of
forests and other natural resources including lakes, rivers, biodiversity and wildlife. The broad
objectives of the Ministry, in a nutshell, are conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests and
wildlife, prevention and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas,
protection of the environment and ensuring the welfare of animals.
4. To attain the above objectives, the Ministry has a broad organizational structure consisting
of a number of Divisions, Attached/Subordinate Offices, Autonomous Institutions, etc. However,
main divisions of the Ministry are : (a) Environment, (b) Forests and Wildlife, (c) National
Afforestation and Eco-development Board, (d) National River Conservation Directorate; and
(e) Animal Welfare.
5. Apart from its Head Office located at New Delhi, the Ministry of Environment and Forests
has six Regional Offices, one each at Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Lucknow, Shillong and
Chandigarh. These Regional Offices perform the functions of monitoring and evaluation of ongoing
forestry development project, particularly, conservation of forests. They also perform functions of
follow up of implementation of conditions and safeguards prescribed by the Ministry while giving
environmental clearance. Besides, the Ministry has eight Subordinate Offices. Under the broad head
of Environment and Ecology, the Ministry has four Autonomous/S tatutory Bodies/Registered
Societies, including 10 Centres of excellence. Under Forestry and Wildlife, it has 8 such
Autonomous Bodies/Registered Societies including 12 Research Institutes/Advanced Centres under
Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education, Dehradun. The Ministry has one Public Sector

6.2 Besides, a special one-time grant of Rs. 50.00 crores to the National Tiger Conservation
Authority to raise, arm and deploy a Special Tiger Protection Force was announced in 2008-09.
In the year 2009-10, similar one time special grant of Rs. 100.00 crores for the Indian Council
of Forestry Research Education, Dehradun and Rs. 15.00 crores each for Botanical Survey of India
and Zoological Survey of India, were announced. Likewise, a special allocation of Rs. 50.00 crores
for cleaning up of important lakes and rivers of historical and cultural importance other than the
Ganga was announced in 2011-12.
6.3 An analysis of the above statement reflects that the Ministry got an approved outlay of
Rs. 10,000.00 crores as Eleventh Plan Outlay plus Rs. 230.00 crores as one time grant during three
financial years of the Plan period. Now, a look at the trend of expenditure shows that while in the
first two years, i.e., 2007-08 and 2008-09, the Ministry was able to utilize the allocated outlay
almost fully, it failed to utilize Rs. 249.31 crores during the year 2009-10. During the year 2011-12,
it was likely to utilize Rs. 1902.00 crores as against the outlay of Rs. 2300.00 crores, thus leaving
Rs. 398.00 crores unutilized. The total outlay remaining unutilized during the Eleventh Plan period
works out to Rs. 1452.98 crores. Although, the Ministry informed that the approved outlay for the
XI Plan 2007-12 of the Ministry was Rs. 10,000.00 crores against which an outlay of Rs. 9231.00
crores was actually allocated in various Annual Plans, the Committee fails to understand as to how
an approved outlay of the Ministry for the entire Plan period got curtailed in various annual Plans
unless Ministry itself was not able to utilize fully the allocated funds leading to reduced allocations
in subsequent years. The Ministry has not given any explanation nor it has informed the Committee
about the steps taken by it to ensure that the approved outlay of the Eleventh Plan period actually
got allocated in successive Annual Plans.
6.4 In any case, even if the actual allocation was reduced from Rs. 10,000 crores to
Rs. 9231.00 crores, the Committee finds that the actual utilisation likely to be made till the end of
the XI Five Year Plan works out to Rs. 8547.02 crores, less by Rs. 683.98 crores. The Ministry,
however, justified the lower utilisation of funds by saying that the gap of approximately Rs. 684.00
crores between outlays allocated and actual expenditure incurred in the Eleventh Plan period is due
to reduction in Ministry’s outlays at Revised Estimates level by around Rs. 628.00 crores and lower
utilisation of funds by the Ministry at the R.E. stage of around of Rs. 56.00 crores. The other
reasons for the underutilization adduced to by the Ministry are – implementing agencies being State
Governments/various Departments whose performance depends on timely release of matching grants;
time lag in release of funds by the Ministry and actual availability of funds to such implementing
agencies and procedural delays, like, delay in receipt of proposals; submission of utilisation
certificates; acquisition of land; completion of works; delays in operationalisation of EAP Projects,
etc. The Committee finds that during the Eleventh Plan period, the progress of utilisation during the
year 2011-12, which is the last and final year of the Eleventh Five Year Plan, is quite discouraging
and tardy. The approved Plan outlay for the year 2011-12 stood at Rs. 2300.00 crores which was
reduced to Rs. 1902.00 crores at the R.E. stage. However, the Committee finds that the actual
expenditure made in the first 11 months of the year, i.e., from April, 2011 to 29
th February, 2012, is
only Rs. 1535.03 crores implying an utilisation ratio of around 81 per cent. The Ministry has, however,
claimed that the remaining amount of Rs. 366.97 crores would be fully utilized by the end of the year.
6.5 The Committee, hopes that the Ministry would not only be able to get full allocation
of its approved budgetary support during the Twelfth Five Year Plan, but would also ensure
full utilisation of funds allocated to it and it would not come to the Committee with same
old excuses for not fully utilizing the allocated funds.

integration of programmes through rationalisation helps the Ministry to focus its
attention on the programmes in an effective, efficient and result oriented manner. But,
at the same, the Committee feels that the smaller sub-schemes after getting integrated
with a major scheme or programme does not attract as much attention and hence its
monitoring and performance gets affected. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
while monitoring the major projects/schemes, the Ministry must ensure that
performance of the smaller sub-schemes is not lost sight of and must ensure that
progress and performance of smaller schemes is also regularly monitored, particularly,
the component of wetlands, scheme of corals and mangroves as these are different from
monitoring an inland lake or river.
7. TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN OUTLAY
7.1 When the Committee enquired from the Ministry about the budgetary allocation made for
the T welfth Five Year Plan (2012-17), it was informed that the outlays for the T welfth Five Year
Plan of the Ministry have not been finalised by the Planning Commission. The Ministry, however,
informed that in its draft proposal for the T welfth Plan submitted to the Planning Commission,
it has proposed an outlay of Rs. 47586.00 crores. It further informed that around 80 per cent
of the estimated fund requirement would be accounted for by 5 major schemes, namely,
Afforestation and Forest Management including Green India Mission; National River Conservation
Plan; including National Ganga River Basin Authority; Project Tiger; Wildlife Management and
Grants-in-Aid to Forestry and Wildlife Institution. On being enquired about the major thrust area
of the Ministry in the T welfth Five Y ear Plan, it was stated that the Approach Paper approved
by the National Development Council in October, 2011 for formulating the T welfth Five Year Plan
has the basic theme as “Faster, Sustainable and more Inclusive Growth”. The Approach Paper
emphasizes, inter-alia , on improving forest cover, preserving wetlands, treatment of municipal
solid waste and urban sewage, restoration of mining areas, protection and preservation of
biodiversity and wildlife, carrying capacity studies in selected river basins, cumulative
environmental impact assessment for vulnerable reasons, maintaining acceptable water quality and
quantity through pollution control of water resources, etc.
7.2 The Committee is surprised to note that the Twelfth Five Year Plan for the Ministry
is yet to be finalised by the Planning Commission even when the first year of the Five Year
Plan has set in. The Committee expresses its serious concern over delay in finalization of
Twelfth Five Y ear Plan outlays of an important Ministry engaged in protection of
environment and conservation of forests, so vital for the healthy and comfortable living of
human beings. The Committee, therefore, recommends that henceforth Planning
Commission must ensure that such sort of delay does not recur in future and outlays are
finalised well before the beginning of the Plan period. The Committee is also of the opinion
that any further laxity in early finalization of Twelfth Plan outlays may have adverse
consequences on restoration of environmental degradation and control of water, air and
noise pollution in particular and, therefore, it should be finalised without any further delay.
The Committee is also of the opinion that environment and forests need to be accorded due
priority in the developmental agenda of the nation in view of the lurking challenges that
climate change poses before us. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the proposed
outlay of Rs. 47586.00 crores of the Ministry should be given serious consideration by the
Planning Commission, so as to ensure availability of adequate funds to the Ministry for
pursuing its avowed objectives successfully.

10. Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)
10.1 Central Pollution Control Board is a technical wing of the Ministry of Environment &
Forests which gets 100 per cent Grants-In-Aid. Prevention and control of environmental pollution
in the country in coordination with the State Pollution Control Boards/Pollution Control Committees
is one of its main responsibilities. In addition to the implementation of Water and Air Acts, CPCB
has mandate for implementation of Rules relating to Hazardous Waste Management, Bio-Medical
Waste, Municipal Solid Waste, Plastic Wastes, etc. in the process of abatement of pollution.
Continuous monitoring of ambient air and water quality, expansion of ambient noise monitoring
network and expansion of manual air and water quality monitoring are amongst other important
functions of the CPCB.
10.2 Some of the important functions of CPCB include:–
• Advise the Central Government on any matter concerning prevention and control of
water and air pollution and improvement of the quality of air;
• Plan and cause to be executed a nation-wide programme for the prevention, control or
abatement of water and air pollution;
• Co-ordinate the activities of the State Board and resolve disputes among them;
• Provide technical assistance and guidance to the State Boards, carry out and sponsor
investigation and research relating to problems of water and air pollution, and for their
prevention, control or abatement;
• Organise through mass media, a comprehensive mass awareness programme on the
prevention, control or abatement of water and air pollution;
• Perform such other function as may be prescribed by the Government of India.
10.3 For the last two years (2010-11 and 2011-12), budgetary outlay (Plan and Non-Plan) for
CPCB has remained the same, i.e., Rs. 62.00 crores. However, this year, there has been a marginal
increase in allocation by Rs. 3.32 crores. The almost stagnant allocation appear in stark contrast
of the pressing need for strengthening the body responsible for combating the rising levels of
pollution throughout the country.
10.4 The Committee further feels that the major constraint in effective functioning of
CPCB is the shortage of technical staff, scientists and lack of quality laboratory facilities.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should focus its attention in
addressing these constraints, so that CPCB is able to effectively discharge its duties and
functions. The Committee also feels that there is a need to improve internal working of the
CPCB and its coordination with SPCBs, etc. The Committee is of the view that CPCB should
hold meetings more frequently and its Members should regularly visit various places and
hold discussion with concerned SPCBs, etc. so as to have a first hand experience of ground
realities prevailing in the country and to sensitize the ground functionaries to effectively
discharge their duties.
10.5 The Committee finds that although pollution in some form or the other has spread its wings
throughout the length and breadth of the country, CPCB, in terms of its infrastructure, manpower,
etc. has not been able to keep pace with the phenomenal growth of the pollution – industrial,
vehicular, sewage and solid waste, etc. It has six zonal offices with each zonal office covering 3
to 8 States while the number of industries, vehicular load, sewage and solid waste, etc. has

14
multiplied manifold in the course of time. The Committee feels that the number of zonal
offices of CPCB needs to be increased so that it is able to keep a closer watch on air, water
and noise pollution in the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry of
Environment & Forests should consider enhancing the number of zonal offices in a phased
but time-bound manner.

10.13 The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry proposes to establish a National

11. National River Conservation Plan
11.1 The National River Conservation Directorate (NRCD) is responsible for administering two

16
Centrally sponsored schemes to improve water quality of polluted stretches of rivers/lakes through
various pollution abatement works, namely, National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) and National
Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystem with National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) and

diversification work to take sewage flowing direct into the rivers for treatment, setting up of

been set up by the Ministry as a registered society to implement the NGRBA Programme in a

th February,
2009. The Authority has both regulatory and developmental functions and will take effective

11.4 The Committee is constrained to observe that despite whatever efforts made hitherto
and a huge investment incurred under various schemes/projects, pollution level in both the
rivers, i.e ., the Ganga and the Yamuna continues to increase unabated. The pathetic
condition of Y amuna which has virtually turned into a ‘Nala’ to carry sewage falling into it
from various drains, is deplorable. The water quality of the Ganga has not shown any
significant improvement either and it is deteriorating day by day. The quality of Ganga
water downstream at several important locations, such as, Kanpur, Allahabad, Varanasi and
Patna still continues to be a major concern for the environmentalist, as well as, the
common man. The Committee feels that one of the reasons for the failure of Government
schemes lies in the fact that Government has so far adopted only engineering centric
approach to solve the problem with undue emphasis on creation of sewage treatment plants,
etc. The Committee feels that engineering centric activities alone will not be successful and
the Ministry should also approach it as a social engineering problem and now the time has
come when we should integrate engineering centric approach with social centric or society
centric approach through which people living on and around the banks of the rivers are
involved and assimilated in the Mission Clean Ganga. The Committee also recommends that
services of various institutes of social sciences, apart from IITs should be sought by the
Government to seek a viable solution of the pollution.
11.5 Yet another reason for the failure of the above programmes undertaken for abatement of
pollution in the river Ganga and Yamuna perhaps lies in the fact that the catchment areas especially
of the river Yamuna has been encroached upon and diverted for construction and developmental
activities. The retention capacity of water/rainwater in the catchment areas has considerably gone
down due to which the river does not get recharged. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Ministry should take steps to stop encroachment and illegal commercial activities
on the catchment areas of all the major rivers including the Ganga and the Yamuna. Yet
another reason for the failure in cleaning the rivers is the day by day dwindling of their
natural flow which has resulted in the assimilating capacity of the river Yamuna almost
coming to a naught and of the river Ganga going down. The Committee is of the opinion
that unless the flow of the river is maintained at a reasonable level, no other effort is going
to be successful. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should pay due
attention on this issue and take steps to ensure that the flow of the river Yamuna and the
Ganga upstream is not disturbed or blocked.

generated from Class-I cities and Class-II towns of the country is estimated to be around 38254

major rivers. The Ministry may coordinate with other concerned Ministries of the
Government of India and State Governments so that coordinated efforts are made to realize
this goal.

12. Environment Impact Assessment
12.1 Environment Impact Assessment is an important tool meant for incorporating environmental
concerns in developmental projects at the Planning Stage. Environmental clearance has been made
mandatory since 1994 in respect of 32 developmental activities including industry, thermal power,
mining, river valley and infrastructure projects, etc. Environmental impact studies are carried out
as per the Environmental Impact Notification 1994 and subsequent assessments which inter-alia
includes public hearing. As per the Environmental Impact Notification, 2006, developmental
activities have been categorized into Category A and Category B based on potential impacts that the
project would have on the environment. Category A projects are appraised at the Central level by
Expert Appraisal Committee, while Category B projects are appraised at the State level by the State
level Expert Appraisal Committee constituted by the Central Government.
12.2 The Committee views environmental assessment as a very important and significant
component of environmental preservation with development. The budgetary allocation under this
Head since 2008-09 has remained stagnant at Rs. 3.50 crores while, the number of applications
for developmental projects have grown manifold. The Committee, however, notes that even the
budgetary allocation of Rs. 3.50 crores last year was not fully utilized and the actual expenditure
as on 29
th February, 2012 under this Head stood at Rs. 2.21 crores. This year, however, there has
been a marginal increase in the allocation which has reached Rs. 3.68 crores from the previous
Rs. 3.50 crores.
12.3 The Committee during its interaction with the other Ministries found that
environmental clearances were being unduly delayed due to lack of infrastructural
facilities and the business as usual approach adopted by the Ministry which is still
following old and outdated methodology for giving these clearances. Moreover, the undue
delays give rise to a public perception that environmental issues are hindering the
development of the country. Such a perception should not be allowed to be created in
public mind as development and environment have to coexist for survival of mankind. It
is unfortunate that the time schedule laid for giving these clearances is rarely adhered
to and it generally takes years to get the required clearances with the result that
developmental work suffer and there is widespread criticism of unduly long period taken
by the Ministry. Conditions laid down while giving environmental clearance which are
necessary for environmental safeguard and mitigating developmental impacts, are not
being properly monitored for the purpose of compliance as a result of which there are a
large number of violations of these conditions.
12.4 The Committee also notes with concern that project proponents themselves are asked to
carry out Environmental Impact Assessment studies at their own cost. State level Members of the
State Level Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) which is constituted by the Central Government
are required to inspect any sight connected with the project or the activity in respect of which
prior environmental clearance is sought with prior notice of at least 7 days to the applicant who
shall provide necessary facilities for the inspection. In the given scenario, it is very difficult to
expect much of the objectivity in preparation of the Environmental Impact Assessment studies and
adherence to the stipulated environmental norms by the project proponents.
12.5 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that there is an urgent need for the
Ministry to streamline its procedures, fix realistic time schedule for giving various
clearances and adhere to those time schedules. The Committee is further of the view that
there should be a system of surprise inspections to check adherence to the conditions laid
while giving clearances and the Environmental Impact Assessment Studies need to be
carried out with greater objectivity.

19
13. Forestry and Wildlife
13.1 Forest forms an integral part of environment and it would not be an exaggeration if it is
said that healthy forests is a sine-quo-non  for healthy environment. Ministry of Environment and
Forests has been pursuing various forestry related programmes to preserve, regenerate and intensify
forest/tree cover in India. In order to promote afforestation tree planting, ecology restoration and
eco development activities in the country, the National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board
(NAEB) was set up in 1992. NAEB is paying special attention to regeneration of degraded forest
areas and lands adjoining forest areas, national parks, sancutries and other protected areas together
with the ecologically fragile areas like the Western Himalayas, Aravalis, Western Ghats, etc. It is
a centrally sponsored programme under which the Ministry is running National Afforestation
Programme, Green India Mission and Intensification of Forest Management Scheme. The
Committee is happy to note that budgetary outlay for the year 2012-13 under forestry and wildlife
has increased from Rs. 927.08 crores in the previous year to Rs. 1077.78 crores which would help
the Ministry to some extent to intensify its forestry efforts. However, this does not appear
sufficient to meet the ambitious target of having 33 per cent geographical area of the country under
tree/forest cover as stipulated in the National Forest Policy, 1988.
13.2 The Committee is further constrained to observe that even after lapse of about 24 years,
this target still appears to be a distant and lofty dream. As per the latest state of Forest Report,
2011, the forest and tree cover in the country constitutes 23.81 per cent of the total geographical
area. It would be relevant to underline here that out of 23.81 per cent, 21.05 per cent is the forest
cover and the rest 2.76 per cent is the tree cover. Out of the 21.05 per cent forest cover, 2.54
per cent is very dense, 9.76 per cent is moderately dense and 8.75 per cent is the open forest.
As per the report, there is a decrease of 367 sq. kms. in country’s forest cover in comparison
to 2009 assessment.
13.3 G reen India Mission – one of the 8 missions under the National Action Plan for climate
change is likely to be launched in 2012-13 which aims to increase forest/tree cover on 5 million
hectare lands and improve quality of forest cover on another 5 million hectare over a period of
ten years with a total cost of 46000.00 crores over a period of ten years. The Committee has been
given to understand that major constraints coming in the way of achieving the forestry target of
33 per cent are the availability of land and financial resources. When the Committee enquired from
the Ministry, whether enough land has been identified and earmarked for the Green India Mission
and if so, what are the details in this regard, the Ministry did not come out with a clear cut reply
which casts serious doubts on the preparations made by the Ministry for the successful completion
of the mission.
13.4 In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment
and Forests should accord priority to regenerate and intensify forestry activities in the
degraded forest areas which are already with the Ministry and in this way the constrain of
non-availability of land could be overcome. The Committee also recommends that the
Ministry should make efforts to get a buffer of forest cover created by those agencies which
require forest land for non-forestry purposes. Ministries of Coal; Power; Steel; etc. may be
involved in this activity, so that, their requirement of forest land for non-forestry purposes
could be met as compensatory afforestation is required to be done by them in advance.
13.5 When the Committee enquired whether Government has revised the target of achieving 33
per cent of forest coverage to the total geographical area of the country and if so what is the
revised target and what factors led to the revision of the target, the Ministry did not come out with
a pointed and specific reply to the above issues and instead gave a general reply that the major
task before the country is to rehabilitate the degraded forest and to enhance the area under forest
and tree cover to 33 per cent of the total geographical area of the country. It also informed that

20
current planting rate of forest and non-forest land is around 1.5 million hectare per annum, etc.
Avoiding direct reply to the specific question suggests that the Ministry has not taken the spirit
behind the question very seriously.  The Committee is of the view that achieving the target of
33 per cent is quite ambitious and very difficult to achieve and, therefore, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry should set a short-term pragmatic target and try to achieve
the long-term target of 33 per cent in a phased manner.
13.6 The Committee finds that under the centrally sponsored scheme of Capacity Building for
Forest Management and Training of Personnel, out of an outlay of Rs. 34.90 crores in 2010-11,
expenditure of Rs. 14.01 crores only could be incurred. Similarly, out of the allocation of Rs. 50.00
crores in 2011-12, reduced to Rs. 36.89 crores at the R.E. stage, the Ministry was able to utilize
only Rs. 18.37 crores which roughly amounts to around 50 per cent of the allocation. Despite the
allocated funds being not fully utilized during the past two years, this year again an outlay of
Rs. 50.00 crores has been made under this Head. The Committee has been informed that these
funds are utilized for patrolling of the forests, establishment of campus, building fire watch towers,
preparation and maintenance of fire line, strengthening forest infrastructure, etc. and hence
constitute an important component of conservation of forests. Similarly, the Committee finds that
as against the outlay of Rs. 65.00 crores under “Intensification of Forest Management’ programme
in the year 2010-11, the actual utilisation remained at Rs. 57.03 crores and out of the allocated
outlay of Rs. 65.00 crores in 2011-12 the Ministry could utilize Rs. 52.23 crores as on 29.2.2012.
Owing to underutilization of allocated funds, the Ministry has failed to achieve the physical targets
in both the years. As regards the target of creation and maintenance of 40,000 kms. of fire lines,
96916 kms. could be created/maintained. Similarly, out of the target of constructing 40,000 forest
boundary pillars, 27,185 pillars alone could be constructed in 2010-11. The Ministry has not
mentioned the achievements in respect of other targets viz. construction of 35 fire watch towers;
300 kms. road, 75 water storage structure and procurement of 100 vehicles, etc. and hence the
Committee does not feel it appropriate to jump on any conclusion. In 2011-12 also, the position
is more or less the same. Out of the target of creating and maintaining fire lines upto 85,929 kms.,
only 52,417 kms. could be created/maintained. 33,137 forest boundary pillars could be constructed
as against the target of 54,323. Out of the target of purchasing/acquiring 195 vehicles, no vehicle
seems to have been procured. The Committee finds that it is the dismal performance on the
part of the Ministry which needs to be improved and intensified in order to protect our
pristine forest cover.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should
make all out efforts to utilize the approved outlay this year and any laxity on the part of
the Ministry would be viewed seriously by the Committee.
14. Corporate Social Responsibility
14.1 The Committee understands that another major constraint in enhancing forest cover in the
country is shortage of adequate funds without which afforestation on a mass scale is not
possible. The Committee also understands that the Ministry cannot manage the required resources
out of the budgetary allocations. It was in this context that the Committee had in its 210
th Report
on Demands for Grants 2010-11 of the Ministry recommended that the Government must make
it mandatory for the public sector undertakings/ major industries in public and private sectors to
spend 50 per cent of the money being spent towards corporate social responsibilities for massive
afforestation under the guidance of the Ministry of Environment and Forests. The Ministry in its
Action Taken Note informed that the matter had been referred to the Ministry of Corporate
Affairs to look into the recommendations of the Committee for making provisions on
afforestation. The Committee in its 219
th Report on Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations Contained in its 210 th Report further reiterated, expressed its dismay over
inaction in the following words:

21
“To make it mandatory for public and private corporates to spend 50% of fund
available for Corporate Social Responsibility for the massive afforestation in the
country, is the policy matter of the Government. Therefore, Parliamentary Standing
Committee directs that in the interest to achieve massive afforestation in the
country, the Ministry of Environment and Forests should approach the competent
authority in Government to formulate the policy. The policy perhaps could be
finalised/agreed at the level of Prime Minister/Cabinet and therefore, the Ministry

further desires that this should be done expeditiously.”
14.2 When the Committee enquired about the latest status of the Action Taken by the Ministry
on the above recommendations of the Committee, the Ministry gave a very general and evasive

14.3 The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the fact that the Ministry
has miserably failed in taking appropriate follow up action and capitalising on the
recommendations of the Committee for arranging additional resources for massive
plantation. The Committee is dismayed to find that the Ministry of Environment and
Forests, instead of being proactive has taken the recommendations of the Committee,
so passively, nonchalantly and causally. The Committee finds that the Ministry has
simply passed the buck on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs and let the matter rest
there.
14.4 It would be pertinent to mention here that the Committee, during its study visit to
Visakhapatnam has successively persuaded major public sector companies like NTPC, HPCL, Vizag
Port Trust and local authorities like Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation, Andhra Pradesh State
Pollution Control Board, etc. to plant 40 lakh plants in a period of 5 years with an investment of
Rs. 600.00 crores and they had willingly agreed to participate in the massive plantation scheme in

15. Wildlife conservation
15.1 The Ministry of Environment and Forests extends technical and financial support to the
State Governments for wildlife conservation under the various centrally sponsored schemes viz.
Integrated Development of Wildlife habitats, Project Tiger, Project Elephant and also through
Central Schemes, i.e. , Strengthening of Wildlife Division and Consultancies for Special Tasks
and through Grants in Aids to the Central Zoo Authority and Wildlife Institute of India,
Dehradun. Our country, at present, has a network of a 668 protected areas out of which 102
are National Parks, 515 Wildlife Sanctuaries, 47 Conservation Reserves and 4 Community
Reserves. Besides, support for protection of wildlife outside protected areas is also given by
the Ministry.

22
16. Project Elephant
16.1 Project Elephant is a centrally sponsored scheme launched by the Government in 1991-92
to protect elephants, their habitats and corridors and to address issues of man – animal conflict.
Presently, the project is being implemented in 18 States/Union Territories. The Ministry has
informed that effective implementation of the Project has over the years resulted in increase in the
population of elephants in the country. The Committee finds that under this Programme, an outlay
of Rs. 21.50 crores both at B.E. and R.E. level was made in the year 2011-12, out of which only
Rs. 13.45 crores has been utilized by the Ministry as on 29
th February, 2012. This year, allocation
under this Head has been marginally increased from Rs. 21.50 crores last year to Rs. 22.58 crores
this year. The Committee recommends that there must not be any let up in the utilisation
of allocated resources under this head as was the case during the year 2011-12 and the
entire outlay should be properly utilized by the Ministry.
17. Project Tiger
17.1 The Centrally sponsored scheme Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to ensure maintenance
of a vital population of tigers for scientific, economic, aesthetic, cultural and ecological values. The
Committee has been informed by the Ministry that this scheme has performed quite well. The
Project Tiger coverage has expanded from the initial 9 tiger reserves to the present 40 reserves
spread over 17 States with a core/critical tiger habitat of 23578.75 kms. and a buffer area of
187.47 sq. kms. Population of tiger in the country has also registered an increase by almost 20
per cent as per an estimate. While the number of tigers was estimated to the 1411 (1165 to 1167
in 2006), it has now gone upto 1706 (1520 – 1909 in 2010). In principle approval has been
accorded by the National Tiger Conservation Authority to create 5 new tiger reserves, one each
in Karnataka, U.P., Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and Rajasthan.
17.2 The Committee finds that allocation under Project Tiger since 2010-11 has been on the
decline. While it was Rs. 243.13 crores at B.E. stage in 2009-10 crores, it came down to 201.50
crores in 2010-11 and further down to 162.72 crores in the year 2011-12. This year the outlay
has registered just a nominal increase which is Rs. 167.70 crores. The Committee finds that the
target of funding support for relocation and rehabilitation of at least 5000 people could not be fully
achieved and rehabilitation of only 2413 families could be undertaken in the year 2010-11.
17.3 However, a newsitem which appeared in the T imes of India on 16.4.2012, citing reply to
a RTI query reveals that over 337 tigers lost their lives in the last decade. The reasons for their
deaths include poaching, infighting accidents and old age among others. According to the newsitem
as many as 68 tigers fell prey to poaching during the period. The highest number of poaching of
tigers was recorded in 2010 when 14 tigers were poached. This number was 13 in 2009, 11 in
2011, 9 in 2022, 6 each in 2007 and 2008. Even the population monitoring methodology adopted
to ascertain the number of tigers in the country has also not been considered to be foolproof by
several experts. When the Committee wanted to know if poaching had emerged as a major
challenge for wildlife protection and whether an allocation of Rs. 6.30 crores for 2012-13 B.E.
under the scheme of Control of Wildlife Crime would be sufficient keeping in view the vulnerability
of wildlife to poaching, the Committee was informed that the allocation made in B.E. 2012-13 is
inadequate to address the issue related to poaching of wildlife in the country.
17.4 The Committee had in its 219
th Report suggested that the Ministry should convince the
Ministry of Finance to enhance allocation of funds for wildlife preservation schemes. When the
Committee enquired about the follow up action taken by the Government on the suggestion and the
details of its outcome, the Ministry informed that the Planning Commission has been requested to
enhance financial allocation under various schemes for wildlife preservation. However, the request
has not yet materialized and response is still awaited. The Committee expresses its deep anguish

23
over a well thought out suggestion/recommendation of the Committee being taken so lightly
and not acceded to even after a lapse of over 16 months and recommends that Planning
Commission should give serious consideration to the need of the Ministry for adequate
funds for preservation and conservation of wildlife. The Committee is of the view that the
reduction in proposed demand of the Ministry of Rs. 1276.30 crores to Rs. 167.70 crores as
final outlay under Project Tiger, is not at all justified. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the proposed allocation of the Ministry should be restored by the Planning
Commission as such a drastic reduction in allocation would badly affect the progress of the
scheme which has raised a lot of hue and cry in the recent years.
18. Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE), Dehradun
18.1 Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE), Dehradun is an autonomous
body under the Ministry of Environment and Forests which was established in 1989 to develop a
holistic forestry research for ensuring scientific management of forests, tree improvement, forest
productivity through scientific and biotechnology research, bioremediation, rehabilitation of
degraded land, conservation of biodiversity, etc. ICFRE has 8 Research Institutes and 4 Advanced
Centres located at Allahabad, Chhindwara, Hyderabad and Aizwal.
18.2 The Committee finds that ICFRE has performed exceedingly well in terms of utilisation of
allocated resources during the entire Eleventh Five Year Plan period. As against an outlay of
Rs. 89.93 crores, actual expenditure reached Rs. 109.93 crores in the year 2009-10, against an
outlay of Rs. 90.00 crores in the year 2010-11, the actual expenditure reached upto Rs. 106.60
crores and in the year 2011-12 it was able to fully utilize the outlay of Rs. 90.00 crores. This year
allocation for ICFRE has marginally increased to Rs. 104.50 crores. While the Committee
appreciates that the trend of expenditure has been very good, its output or results have not been
discernable or significant in terms of its mandate. The Ministry of Environment and Forests is still
struggling to achieve the objective 33 per cent forest coverage to the total geographical area of the
country. Deforestation and degeneration of forests still continue to be major problems. The
Committee feels that during the last almost 23 years of its existence, ICFRE should have
made significant contribution in conservation of forests and rehabilitation of degraded land
and established itself as a premier research institute on the pattern of CSIR, which has
made remarkable achievement in scientific and technological development of the country.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that ICFRE should galvanize its resources in such
a manner as to provide viable solutions for the problems afflicting the goal of preservation
of forests and rehabilitation of degraded land, so that, the green/forest cover of the country
could be substantially enhanced.
19. Biodiversity
19.1 India is a mega diverse country and is rich in biodiversity (8 per cent of the World). Taking
cognizance of the International Convention on Biodiversity and to address the excessive pressure
on biodiversity, Government has enacted Biological Diversity Act, 2002 in pursuance of which a
3 tier mechanism has been provided – National Biodiversity Authority at the National level, the State
Biodiversity Board at the State level and Biodiversity Management Committees at the Panchayat
level. National Biodiversity Authority is a body corporate, autonomous regulatory organisation
constituted under Section 8 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 to implement its provisions. The
vision of National Biodiversity Authority is conservation and sustainable use of India’s rich
biodiversity and associated knowledge with peoples’ participation. Its mission inter-alia  is to
contribute towards the prevention of misappropriation of bio-resources and provide policy and
support relating to conservation, sustainable use of its components and equitable sharing of benefits
arising out of utilisation of biological resources.

24
19.2 The Committee finds that this year, no budgetary allocation has been made under the
scheme of biodiversity conservation and rural livelihood improvement project and enquired from the
Ministry if this programme has been discontinued this year. The Ministry informed the Committee
that this programme has not been discontinued. It is an externally aided project which commenced
its operations only on 13
th July, 2011 with World Bank assistance. The duration of the project is
6 years with a total outlay of Rs. 137.35 crores and for the current financial year, an amount of
Rs. 2.388 crores has been released to the implementing agencies for the implementation of the
project.
19.3 The Committee is constrained to observe that although Biological Diversity Act was
enacted in 2002, it is yet to be fully implemented. State Biodiversity Board have so far been
set up by 25 States while 3 States viz. Bihar, Maharashtra and J&K are yet to set up their
State Boards. Only 14 States have so far notified the State specific rules in accordance with
the Section 63(1) of the Act. So far, over 31,000 Biodiversity Management Committees have
been constituted by the local bodies in 14 States. It shows lack of seriousness both on the
part of the Central Government and the State Governments towards the implementation of
the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry
should actively pursue this matter with the State Government to set up their State Boards
and particularly, Panchayat level Biodiversity Management Committees which give sanction
and agree on benefits sharing agreement, so that they are activated and constituted at the
earliest.
19.4 The Committee feels that conservation of biodiversity provides not only several goods and
services required for human survival, but also livelihood to people and contributes to sustainable
development and poverty alleviation. India is a party to the Cartagena protocol on bio-safety which
was negotiated under the aegis of the Convention on Biological Diversity. Convention on biological
diversity is the first comprehensive global agreement which addresses all aspects relating to
biodiversity. The Committee was informed that India is hosting global biodiversity summit known
as the 11
th Conference of Parties (COP-11) in October, 2012 at Hyderabad, which will enable India
to be President of COP for two years and play major role in setting up of a global agency on
biodiversity in the context of sustainable livelihoods. While, the Committee appreciates that India
is actively and effectively participating in this international conference being held at Hyderabad, it
feels that the Ministry needs to further strengthen its Biodiversity Scheme/ Genetic Engineering
Approval Committee, so that, it could arrive at a final decision on commercial release of transgenic/
G .M. Crops. Moratorium on B.T. Brinjal has put the whole area of biotechnology in a limbo.
Scientists, students, etc. engaged in this field are worried about the future of biotechnology in
India. On the other hand, bio-safety aspects of the notification of genetically modified seeds is also
a matter of serious concern which has the potential to adversely affecting farmers, crops, labours.
In such a situation, the Committee feels that there is an urgent need to develop strong and
impartial regulatory mechanism which could inspire confidence in the public, so that,
decision taken by it enjoy credibility of all the stakeholders.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
1. The Committee, hopes that the Ministry would not only be able to get full allocation
of its approved budgetary support during the Twelfth Five Year Plan, but would also ensure
full utilisation of funds allocated to it and it would not come to the Committee with same
old excuses for not fully utilizing the allocated funds. (Para 6.5)
2. The Committee is of the view that integration of programmes through rationalisation
helps the Ministry to focus its attention on the programmes in an effective, efficient and
result oriented manner. But, at the same, the Committee feels that the smaller sub-
schemes after getting integrated with a major scheme or programme does not attract as
much attention and hence its monitoring and performance gets affected. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that while monitoring the major projects/ schemes, the Ministry
must ensure that performance of the smaller sub-schemes is not lost sight of and must
ensure that progress and performance of smaller schemes is also regularly monitored,
particularly, the component of wetlands, scheme of corals and mangroves as these are
different from monitoring an inland lake or river. (Para 6.9)
3. The Committee is surprised to note that the Twelfth Five Year Plan for the Ministry
is yet to be finalised by the Planning Commission even when the first year of the Five Year
Plan has set in. The Committee expresses its serious concern over delay in finalization of
Twelfth Five Year Plan outlays of an important Ministry engaged in protection of
environment and conservation of forests, so vital for the healthy and comfortable living of
human beings. The Committee, therefore, recommends that henceforth Planning
Commission must ensure that such sort of delay does not recur in future and outlays are
finalised well before the beginning of the Plan period. The Committee is also of the opinion
that any further laxity in early finalization of Twelfth Plan outlays may have adverse
consequences on restoration of environmental degradation and control of water, air and
noise pollution in particular and therefore it should be finalised without any further delay.
The Committee is also of the opinion that environment and forests need to be accorded due
priority in the developmental agenda of the nation in view of the lurking challenges that
climate change poses before us. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the proposed
outlay of Rs. 47586.00 crores of the Ministry should be given serious consideration by the
Planning Commission, so as to ensure availability of adequate funds to the Ministry for
pursuing its avowed objectives successfully. (Para 7.2)
4. The Committee is constrained to observe that this is a very disturbing trend which
needs to be reversed. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission
must provide not only adequate Budgetary Support to the Ministry of Environment and
Forests at the R.E. stage of this Financial Y ear, but also seriously consider substantially
enhancing the percentage share of Ministry of Environment and Forests in the Central Plan
consistent with the growing importance of issues dealt by the Ministry. (Para 8.9)
5. The Committee feels that the tardy trend of utilisation of resources provides the
Planning Commission with an alibi to affect cut in the allocation of resources. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should make necessary efforts to fully
utilize the allocated resources in future, so that, Planning Commission does not take
recourse to such cut measures. (Para 8.13)

26
6. The Committee feels that reduction in Budgetary Allocations is hardly justified as it
will adversely affect environment and forestry activities. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that adequate budgetary support should be provided to the Ministry at the R.E.
level. (Para 8.16)

CPCB is the shortage of technical staff, scientists and lack of quality laboratory facilities.

consider enhancing the number of zonal offices in a phased but time-bound manner.
(Para 10.5)

the Planning Commission did not allocate adequate resources for prevention and control of
pollution.  The Committee also recommends that sufficient budgetary allocation should be
allocated under this Head by the Planning Commission, so that the Ministry could take
effective measures to deal with the ever increasing problem of pollution. (Para 10.7)

somewhere in the Sixth Five Year Plan under Ganga Action Plan. Thereafter, Ganga Action

16. The Committee is constrained to observe that despite whatever efforts made hitherto
and a huge investment incurred under various schemes/projects, pollution level in both the
rivers, i.e. , the Ganga and the Y amuna continues to increase unabated. The pathetic

the Ministry should also approach it as a social engineering problem and now the time has
come when we should integrate engineering centric approach with social centric or society
centric approach through which people living on and around the banks of the rivers are
involved and assimilated in the Mission Clean Ganga. The Committee also recommends that
services of various institutes of social sciences, apart from IITs should be sought by the
Government to seek a viable solution of the pollution. (Para 11.4)
17. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take steps to stop
encroachment and illegal commercial activities on the catchment areas of all the major
rivers including the Ganga and the Yamuna. Y et another reason for the failure in cleaning
the rivers is the day by day dwindling of their natural flow which has resulted in the
assimilating capacity of the river Yamuna almost coming to a naught and of the river Ganga
going down. The Committee is of the opinion that unless the flow of the river is maintained
at a reasonable level, no other effort is going to be successful. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should pay due attention on this issue and take steps to
ensure that the flow of the river Yamuna and the Ganga upstream is not disturbed or
blocked. (Para 11.5)
18. The Committee notes with concern slow progress in enhancing the sewage treatment
facilities and fears that unless problem is tackled with seriousness and urgency, the gap
would further widen in view of the growing urbanisation and, therefore, recommends that

28
the Ministry should intensify its efforts for building enough treatment capacity to bridge the
gap between the sewage treatment and sewage generation in a time bound manner in cities
situated on the bank of major rivers. The Ministry may coordinate with other concerned
Ministries of the Government of India and State Governments so that coordinated efforts
are made to realize this goal. (Para 11.6)
19. The Committee during its interaction with the other Ministries found that
environmental clearances were being unduly delayed due to lack of infrastructural facilities
and the business as usual approach adopted by the Ministry which is still following old and
outdated methodology for giving these clearances. Moreover, the undue delays give rise to
a public perception that environmental issues are hindering the development of the country.
Such a perception should not be allowed to be created in public mind as development and
environment have to coexist for survival of mankind. It is unfortunate that the time
schedule laid for giving these clearances is rarely adhered to and it generally takes years
to get the required clearances with the result that developmental work suffer and there is
widespread criticism of unduly long period taken by the Ministry. Conditions laid down while
giving environmental clearance which are necessary for environmental safeguard and
mitigating developmental impacts, are not being properly monitored for the purpose of
compliance as a result of which there are a large number of violations of these conditions.
(Para 12.3)
20. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that there is an urgent need for the
Ministry to streamline its procedures, fix realistic time schedule for giving various
clearances and adhere to those time schedules. The Committee is further of the view that
there should be a system of surprise inspections to check adherence to the conditions laid
while giving clearances and the Environmental Impact Assessment Studies need to be
carried out with greater objectivity. (Para 12.5)
21. In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment
and Forests should accord priority to regenerate and intensify forestry activities in the
degraded forest areas which are already with the Ministry and in this way the constrain of
non-availability of land could be overcome. The Committee also recommends that the
Ministry should make efforts to get a buffer of forest cover created by those agencies which
require forest land for non-forestry purposes. Ministries of Coal; Power; Steel; etc. may be
involved in this activity, so that, their requirement of forest land for non-forestry purposes
could be met as compensatory afforestation is required to be done by them in advance.
(Para 13.4)
22. The Committee is of the view that achieving the target of 33 per cent is quite
ambitious and very difficult to achieve and, therefore, the Committee recommends that the
Ministry should set a short-term pragmatic target and try to achieve the long-term target
of 33 per cent in a phased manner. (Para 13.5)
23. The Committee finds that it is the dismal performance on the part of the Ministry
which needs to be improved and intensified in order to protect our pristine forest cover. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should make all out efforts to utilize
the approved outlay this year and any laxity on the part of the Ministry would be viewed
seriously by the Committee. (Para 13.6)
24. “To make it mandatory for public and private Corporates to spend 50% of fund
available for Corporate Social Responsibility for the massive afforestation in the country, is
the policy matter of the Government. Therefore, Parliamentary Standing Committee directs
that in the interest to achieve massive afforestation in the country, the Ministry of

29
Environment and Forests should approach the competent authority in Government to
formulate the policy. The policy perhaps could be finalised/agreed at the level of Prime
Minister/Cabinet and therefore, the Ministry should approach this competent authority to
formulate the policy. The Committee further desires that this should be done expeditiously.”
(Para 14.1)
25. The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the fact that the Ministry has
miserably failed in taking appropriate follow up action and capitalising on the
recommendations of the Committee for arranging additional resources for massive plantation.
The Committee is dismayed to find that the Ministry of Environment and Forests, instead
of being proactive has taken the recommendations of the Committee, so passively,
nonchalantly and causally. The Committee finds that the Ministry has simply passed the
buck on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs and let the matter rest there. (Para 14.3)
26. The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of adopting a casual and callous
approach to the recommendations of the Committee, the Ministry should proactively
organise meeting with all the stakeholders and persuade them to voluntarily participate in
the mass plantation movement. (Para 14.4)
27. The Committee recommends that there must not be any let up in the utilisation of
allocated resources under this head as was the case during the year 2011-12 and the entire
outlay should be properly utilized by the Ministry. (Para 16.1)
28. The Committee expresses its deep anguish over a well thought out suggestion/
recommendation of the Committee being taken so lightly and not acceded to even after a
lapse of over 16 months and recommends that Planning Commission should give serious
consideration to the need of the Ministry for adequate funds for preservation and
conservation of wildlife. The Committee is of the view that the reduction in proposed
demand of the Ministry of Rs. 1276.30 crores to Rs. 167.70 as final outlay under Project
Tiger, is not at all justified. The Committee, therefore, recommends that \he proposed
allocation of the Ministry should be restored by the Planning Commission as such a drastic
reduction in allocation would badly affect the progress of the scheme which has raised a lot
of hue and cry in the recent years. (Para 17.4)
29. The Committee feels that during the last almost 23 years of its existence, ICFRE
should have made significant contribution in conservation of forests and rehabilitation of
degraded land and established itself as a premier research institute on the pattern of CSIR,
which has made remarkable achievement in scientific and technological development of the
country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that ICFRE should galvanize its resources
in such a manner as to provide viable solutions for the problems afflicting the goal of
preservation of forests and rehabilitation of degraded land, so that, the green/forest cover
of the country could be substantially enhanced. (Para 18.2)
30. The Committee is constrained to observe that although Biological Diversity Act was
enacted in 2002, it is yet to be fully implemented. State Biodiversity Board have so far been
set up by 25 States while 3 States viz. Bihar, Maharashtra and J&K are yet to set up their
State Boards. Only 14 States have so far notified the State specific rules in accordance with
the Section 63(1) of the Act. So far, over 31,000 Biodiversity Management Committees have
been constituted by the local bodies in 14 States. It shows lack of seriousness both on the
part of the Central Government and the State Governments towards the implementation of
the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry
should actively pursue this matter with the State Government to set up their State Boards
and particularly, Panchayat level Biodiversity Management Committees which give sanction

30
and agree on benefits sharing agreement, so that they are activated and constituted at the
earliest. (Para 19.3)
31. In such a situation, the Committee feels that there is an urgent need to develop
strong and impartial regulatory mechanism which could inspire confidence in the public, so
that, decision taken by it enjoy credibility of all the stakeholders. (Para 19.4)
